engineering.title: The production system behind this demo
engineering.lead: Abosefen runs a real sanitaryware shop in Cairo: the online store, the counter, the warehouse and the books. This demo shows the storefront and part of the back office. This page shows what runs behind them, the hard problems it solves, and how each solution is proved.
engineering.by: Designed, directed and shipped by Antonious Shehata, 2026 — built with AI-assisted development.
engineering.numbersNote: Counted in the private repository in October 2026. C# lines leave out generated database migrations; tests are the cases of one full run.

stats.rules: business rules written down, 180 enforced in code

engineering.archLead: Ten services behind one gateway. Each service owns its data, and they talk through events, so a slow e-mail never holds up a sale.

arch.label: Architecture of the production system
arch.legend: Solid lines: HTTP requests · dashed lines: events and internal calls

archPoints.p1: Every service has its own PostgreSQL database and its own migrations. Reports in the back office read the other databases read-only; they never write to them.
archPoints.p2: The gateway is the only door. It checks the token and the permissions, limits the rate per visitor, enforces the shop's launch stage (closed → browse → order requests → full shop), and answers 404 for every internal route.
archPoints.p3: Services publish events to one RabbitMQ topic exchange through an outbox, so a change and its event are saved together. Failed messages wait in a dead-letter queue that the back office can replay.
archPoints.p4: Two Python workers do the heavy reading on the same small server: OCR for suppliers' price lists, and image vectors for search by photo. No paid AI service is involved.

engineering.casesTitle: Eight hard problems, and how each is solved
engineering.casesLead: Each one is a real situation from the shop. The code excerpts are shortened from the private repository.

money.title: Money can't be booked twice
money.problem: Two tills can pay the same supplier at the same instant, write the same cheque number, or cash a cheque while someone else cancels it. Checks made before saving can both pass.
money.s1: Every save that names a supplier or a worker first takes a PostgreSQL advisory lock on that person, held until the transaction ends. Saves for one person run one after another.
money.s2: Under the lock the facts are read again: what the supplier is still owed, and whether the cheque still stands and is not yet cashed. If anything changed, nothing is saved.
money.s3: Partial unique indexes are the last wall: one cheque number while it stands, one cashing per cheque, one supplier invoice number a year. Voucher numbers come from a database counter with no gaps.
money.proof: Unit tests cover each rule. A rehearsal script fires the races at a copy of the real PostgreSQL database: a cheque cancelled and cashed at the same instant, three times, and never both. The unit tests run on an in-memory database, where locks do nothing; that is why the races are rehearsed on PostgreSQL.

month.title: Closing a month without stopping the shop
month.problem: Once a month's VAT return is filed, nothing may be dated into it. But a month could close between a save reading the calendar and committing, and events that arrive late still need a home.
month.s1: There is one calendar key. Every posting holds it shared; closing or reopening a month holds it alone. No month closes between a save's read and its commit.
month.s2: An entry typed by hand into a closed month is refused. An entry a service reports late is booked at noon of the first open day, because midnight in Cairo is still the day before in UTC, and it keeps its document's own date.
month.s3: Months close in an unbroken run. Only the last one can be reopened, with a reason, and both actions are written to the audit log.
month.proof: Tests: a month closes only after it ends and in order; nothing is typed into a closed month; a late system entry moves to the first open day and keeps its date; debts are aged by the paper's own date.

oneDoor.title: One reader, one door
oneDoor.problem: A supplier once had three different balances (the catalogue's, the payables page's and the books') and two places where a payment could be typed, so one instalment could be recorded twice.
oneDoor.s1: Balance, statement and payables ageing are all read from one place: the ledger lines on Accounts Payable tagged with that supplier. A cancelled voucher and its mirror entry drop out together.
oneDoor.s2: The old payment endpoint of the catalogue service now answers 410 Gone and says where to go. The day-book is the only door.
oneDoor.s3: Stock follows the same idea: goods leave the shelf only when an order's reservation is confirmed. Every sale path goes through it, and asking twice deducts once.
oneDoor.proof: A guard test fails the build if the catalogue gets a payment method back, if its old route stops answering 410, or if any screen reads the catalogue's own balance again. Stock tests check that a repeated confirmation deducts once.

revision.title: A decision is tied to what was read
revision.problem: A customer can edit a review while the shop is pressing "Publish". Without a guard, words nobody in the shop had read would go live.
revision.s1: Every review carries a revision number that goes up with every edit and every decision. EF Core uses it as a concurrency token, so the database refuses a save made on an older read.
revision.s2: The publish request must carry the revision the screen showed. A different one is answered 409, "changed since you read it".
revision.s3: A writer's edit that crosses a decision is applied on top of it and goes back to waiting. Nothing is published that was not read.
revision.proof: Tests slip a second database context in during the save: publishing unread words is refused, and two decisions at the same time become one, with the second asked to read again.

audit.title: An audit log that can't publish a refused change
audit.problem: The audit record used to be saved through the request's own database context, which could still hold a change the endpoint had refused. Saving the audit row would have saved that change too. A code review caught it.
audit.s1: The audit record is now written in a database scope of its own, through the outbox, never through the request's.
audit.s2: Only changes are recorded. A question asked with POST (a count, a preview, a photo search) is marked as not audited, and a dry run says it only asked.
audit.s3: A bulk change leaves a note made only of numbers and ids. A sentence or a typed name is dropped, so the log never repeats personal data.
audit.proof: An architecture test calls an endpoint that adds a row and answers 400: the row is not saved, the audit event is. A second test reads the source and fails the build if any middleware is handed the request's database context or outbox.

search.title: Search the way Egyptians type
search.problem: Shoppers mix alef and hamza forms, ⁨ة⁩ and ⁨ه⁩, ⁨ى⁩ and ⁨ي⁩, Arabic-Indic digits, trade slang and half-typed words. Exact matching found nothing: ⁨«بان»⁩ returned no results instead of bathtubs.
search.s1: One fold function is written twice, in C# and as a PostgreSQL function, so the database and the app agree on every letter. Products carry a folded search text that triggers keep current.
search.s2: A short word that the catalogue never holds whole, but that starts some of its words, is read as a word still being typed: ⁨«بان»⁩ finds ⁨بانيو⁩, never a word with ⁨«بان»⁩ in the middle.
search.s3: The search learns. Every query is counted, searches with no result show the shop what customers ask for and it does not stock, an accepted "did you mean" becomes a synonym, and the owner can teach word pairs.
search.proof: Tests check that the C# rule and the database's own regular expression give the same answer. A measuring tool runs the shop's real searches before every release.

photo.title: Search by photo with no paid AI
photo.problem: Customers wanted to photograph a part and find it, without a cloud AI bill, without API keys, without storing their photos, and on the same small server that runs the shop.
photo.s1: A Python worker runs DINOv2-small as ONNX on the CPU and turns every catalogue picture into a vector of 384 numbers. A background job keeps the index current.
photo.s2: A search compares the photo with the whole library in memory (SIMD dot products, no vector database), removes hidden products before ranking, and keeps only close matches.
photo.s3: The photo comes from the camera or the gallery only. It is never written to disk, its type is judged by its bytes and not its name, and the gateway limits how often a visitor can search.
photo.proof: Tests: hidden products never appear, vectors from another model find nothing, a file is judged by its magic bytes. An integration test runs the library on real PostgreSQL. The model was chosen by measuring it against CLIP on the shop's own photos.

rules.title: Rules the code enforces, and changes rehearsed before they ship
rules.problem: The owner's business rules lived in conversations. A rule that lives only in someone's head is broken by the next change, and a money bug found after release is found by a customer.
rules.s1: 200 rules are written down, each naming the class or test that refuses a violation. Guard tests read the code itself: for example, only one service may write stock movements, and every message the server sends exists in Arabic, English and German.
rules.s2: A change to money, stock or the books passes six gates: agreed first, a failing test first, an independent review on file, a rehearsal on a copy of the data, a walk through the screens in Arabic on phone and desktop, and a books check after the deploy.
rules.s3: Deploys are built from a clean archive of one commit. Every image carries its commit, and a check lists any service still running older code.
rules.proof: The gates catch real faults. On 14 October 2026 the review found a cheque that could be cashed while it was being cancelled, and the books check on the rehearsal copy found a supplier's opening balance counted wrongly. Both were fixed, with tests, before release.

ai.title: How AI is used
ai.text: I own the product: the requirements, the 200 business rules, the priorities, the reviews on screen and every release decision. AI pair-programming (Claude Code) writes and checks code under that direction, the way modern teams work — and the guardrails on this page (written rules, guard tests, six gates, rehearsals on a copy of the data) are how its work is held to the standard before anything reaches the shop.

tests.title: Tests at three levels
tests.text: About 2,000 unit test methods (xUnit) that run to 5,314 cases; integration tests on real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ in containers (Testcontainers); and rehearsals on a copy of the production data for anything that touches money.

security.title: Secure by default
security.text: Short-lived JWTs with a rotating refresh token per device, stored hashed; BCrypt passwords; permissions checked per section and action; rate limits at the gateway; internal routes hidden. CI runs secret scanning, dependency review and vulnerability checks.

arabic.title: Arabic first
arabic.text: Right to left by default, in three languages from translation files. Audits fail the build on text written outside them. The owner types Arabic only; the program writes the English and German and he can correct them.

oneShop.title: Built with one real shop
oneShop.text: The owner's words became the category tree, the rules and the search vocabulary. The program proposes and he decides: nothing in the catalogue is moved without his say.

engineering.note: Code excerpts are shortened from the private repository; no data of the shop or its customers appears here. This demo is a separate, standalone app that shares no code with production.

latest.title: Latest in production
latest.lead: What changed in the real system most recently. When a change can be shown with invented data, the demo gets its own version of it the same day.

understoodSearch.title: The search knows what it asks for — the thing itself first
understoodSearch.text: Every product is read as a merchant reads it: by the thing its name begins with (⁨«حوض مطبخ»⁩ is a sink; ⁨«مصفاة حوض مطبخ»⁩ a strainer, though it holds both words). A search is read the same way in Arabic, English and German, and the products that ARE the thing asked for come first. In production: about 150 kinds across every department, each product’s reading kept and read again by itself when the product or the knowledge changes — ⁨«Toilette»⁩ now opens with toilets, not a paper holder.

threeLanguages.title: One search in Arabic, English and German
threeLanguages.text: The same rules in every language: Arabic is found after its article, a German part inside the word it builds (⁨«Armatur»⁩ in ⁨«Waschtischarmatur»⁩), an English word only whole (⁨«bath»⁩ never inside ⁨«bathroom»⁩). In production the German names joined the search text gradually, the search answering all along.

amazonOrder.title: Like Amazon: the product asked for first
amazonOrder.text: Among products found equally well: the owner’s pick, then a product before its spare part, the category most results are of, a listing with a photo and a price, the most viewed — and the same name never twice in a row. A name that says the opposite of a word typed comes after.

searchWatch.title: The search is watched on the real catalogue
searchWatch.text: After every deploy and every six hours the program searches its own shop as a customer: the trade’s words with the fewest and the most results they may bring, every search a customer made that found products, the sorted list and the categories against the search, codes and hidden products. A failure is on the owner’s screen at once, and a deploy waits for the first round.

listKit.title: One way every list searches, pages and dates
listKit.text: Every list — on the server and on the screens — now searches, pages and filters by date one way: every word in any order, a code without its dashes, a whole Cairo day, the newest question wins. Tests fail the build when a new screen writes its own.

marketWords.title: Search reads the trade's own words
marketWords.text: ⁨«كرسي»⁩ finds toilets, ⁨«نيبل»⁩ finds what is written ⁨«نبل»⁩, ⁨«بي بي ار»⁩ finds PPR and ⁨«اطقم»⁩ finds sets. In production too: a word typed alone is looked for even when it usually only describes, a sorted search counts everything it found, and a correction shoppers accepted waits for the owner before it changes what any word means.

categoryFilters.title: Category filters that keep their word
categoryFilters.text: Filters live in the page's address, so «back» from a product keeps them and another category starts clean. Every maker, size and finish of the whole category is counted on the server, and a filter is offered only when its data is real.

wordStart.title: A short word finds the words it begins
wordStart.text: Typing ⁨«بان»⁩ now finds ⁨بانيو⁩ and ⁨«حو»⁩ finds ⁨حوض⁩, while a short word never matches inside another word.

supplierCheques.title: Cheques to suppliers, and suppliers' opening balances
supplierCheques.text: A cheque carries its number and due date and is cashed once; a cheque cancelled at the moment it is cashed is never both. Opening balances of suppliers, and each supplier entered once.

categoryPictures.title: Every category has a picture
categoryPictures.text: Thirty-one empty categories took a picture of their own type, each one checked by eye; the web is now one of the sources.

productReading.title: The program reads a product like a merchant
productReading.text: It reads a product's name as kind, material, colour and joint, proposes its category, and learns from what the owner teaches it. Nothing moves without his say.

reviews.title: Reviews wait for the shop
reviews.text: A review is published only after the shop reads it, and waits again when its writer changes it; «verified purchase» is read from the orders' books.

siteNumbers.title: The site counts its own visits
siteNumbers.text: Visits and purchases counted by the shop itself, with no cookie and nothing kept about the person; the owner decides what customers see.

jobs.title: Jobs: the owner posts an ad, people apply, the team calls them
jobs.text: The owner writes a job ad in Arabic and the program words its English and German; a «Jobs» page anyone applies from in a minute — even while the shop is closed — with a name, an Egyptian mobile and a governorate, and an applications screen with a badge for the new ones and a call or WhatsApp in one tap. Photos of a CV stay closed until the owner turns them on with one switch; then they are cleaned of camera data by the same code that cleans customers’ photos.

everyLevelSearch.title: Search at every level: whatever a worker knows of a thing finds it
everyLevelSearch.text: An invoice by its number typed without dashes, by the customer’s phone typed any way (010… or +20…), or by a product on it under today’s name in any language or its code — though the line keeps the name it was sold under. In production: invoices, price statement requests, returns, purchases, transfers, deliveries, the day-book, receivables and payables, and Ctrl K searches every list at once. Try it here on the back office’s orders.

hiddenOptions.title: A hidden option is the team’s — a shopper never finds the product by it
hiddenOptions.text: A colour or size the team hid on a product was still in its search text: a shopper found the product by its colour, code or barcode. Now every product has two texts: the shown one everybody searches, the hidden one only the team — proved on a real PostgreSQL.

marketingMenu.title: Ads, coupons and points are a menu group of their own
marketingMenu.text: On the owner’s word, the marketing screens left «Sales» for a «Marketing» group — and the menu is still guarded by a check that refuses a group of more than nine links or a link without its name in three languages.

categoryPricing.title: Each company priced category by category — the owner’s two ways, its cost kept
categoryPricing.text: The owner picks a company and sees only its categories, as a tree; he ticks some and gives them a way: «a discount on the list» (cost = the list less his discount, sale = the list less the customer’s) or «net + profit». A category without one takes the one above it, then the company’s. The list price is kept on every product and colour, so a changed rule is priced again, reviewed before it applies and undone at will; the company’s sheet goes out as Excel and comes back edited; the purchase invoice proposes the cost from the list. The cost is seen only by who may change prices or buy — rehearsed on a copy of the real catalogue: a first re-pricing changed 0 of 3,921 prices. A list may hold the 14 % VAT or not: each company has a switch and each list may say otherwise, and a purchase tax invoice is proposed the cost without the VAT, since it adds it below.

priceListsPlain.title: The price-lists committee: each list says what it waits for
priceListsPlain.text: The owner found the price lists hard, so a committee of the people who use them (purchasing, pricing, catalogue, accounts, sales, testing) read them end to end: each list now says its next step in words with «needs your decision» first, its lines in three plain groups (sure / to look at / no product found), an unsure line shows the product’s photo with «right / wrong» in one tap, a re-pricing that changes nothing makes no list, and «the lists still missing» per company.

shopDays.title: The day is the shop’s — Cairo’s, not Greenwich’s
shopDays.text: The books, the stock and the money totals cut the day at UTC midnight (02:00 or 03:00 in the shop): a sale at 00:30 landed on the day before, «to day X» lost the whole last day, and a stock card asked from a day began at zero. Now the day page, trial balance, income statement, balance sheet, debt ages, reports and revenue read Cairo’s day, the stock card opens with its opening balance, a coupon runs whole days and every document number takes the shop’s year. Done through the six gates: tests that failed on the old code, a five-direction review, a rehearsal on a copy of the data.

reportsFromBooks.title: The dashboard and the reports read the books
reportsFromBooks.text: The dashboard read a separate tally nothing filled, so it showed zero while the books held the month’s invoices. Now the month’s revenue, the invoice count and average, and the sales, purchases and cash-flow reports are read from the books by the shop’s day: invoices after discounts, returns and cancellations, before VAT — the income statement’s figure to the piastre — and purchases on the day they were received. The owner was asked first; a test failed on the old code; a five-direction review; a rehearsal on a copy of the data.

phoneMenu.title: The phone menu fits one screen
phoneMenu.text: It was eleven rows one under the other. Now: a greeting with your name, the team’s panel as one button, your account’s pages as tiles three a row (orders, price statements, favourites with their count, points, e-mail settings), then «Shop» with four links. It opens right under the bar instead of under the language button. The owner saw it in two screenshots before it went live.

marketFold.title: The dollar and gold watch folds and opens
marketFold.text: On the dashboard, the market card (dollar, euro, copper, gold) now has an arrow beside its title: folded it is one line with the title and the last update, and it opens back as it was. Each device remembers the choice. On the price-freshness page it stays open, since there it is the subject. And the big title card at the top of the dashboard is gone, at the owner’s word: the bar and the side menu already name the page, so it now opens on the shortcuts. The «back to the shop» button beside the search went too: the shop’s own bar always sits above the panel.

panelStrip.title: The panel’s menu became a strip of icons
panelStrip.text: On a laptop the long menu (14 groups and a block of pinned tiles) is now a narrow strip: «Pinned», then each group as its icon over its name. A press opens the group’s pages beside the strip, over the page; choosing a page, Escape or a press outside closes it, and the page keeps the width the old menu took. Groups went from 14 to 11; barcode printing stays one press. A phone keeps its drawer. The owner saw three ways, asked to see this one on the real screen, then approved it. The design audit now refuses a bottom bar that writes the side’s width as a number of its own. And on the phone: ☰ opens the eleven sections as tiles, three a row, on one screen; a section shows its pages with «All sections» to go back, and the pinned pages stay in the bottom bar.

stockCounts.title: Stock counts in sessions: workers count blind, only the owner writes
stockCounts.text: A supervisor opens a count on a warehouse's shelves. A worker counts on his phone by pictures: the shelf's big number in its room's colour, scan the shelf label (a wrong shelf turns red with a buzz), every scanned piece shows the product's photo and a big number, with − / + and a digits-only pad. He never sees the books (a blind count). Finishing a shelf writes the books' quantity beside each line; what the books hold but nobody found counts as zero. «Count differences» are priced at today's cost, and «Approve» is the owner's alone: written shelf by shelf, each shelf whole or not at all, and sales made after the count are not counted twice. An independent review found 2 blockers and 7 fixes — all fixed — and a rehearsal on a database copy found two more (one in the stock door itself), fixed with tests. Then, from the owner trying it: a shelf taken by mistake can be let go (it waits again for its label, nothing in stock moves); a 🔊 beside every sentence and name reads it aloud with the phone’s best voice (an Egyptian one first, and a «Choose the voice» sheet to try the others), the spoken sentences written with their vowels; and a barcode nobody knows is looked up by name or number. And, at the owner’s word on the cost of a first count («keep it zero, with the possibility to edit it»): a product counted for the first time in a warehouse is worth 0 until the owner types its cost per piece before «Approve» — written as its opening balance (the owner’s equity), also for pieces sold before it was ever counted. The independent review found that case (a blocker) and two smaller ones; all fixed, with tests that failed first, and tried on a database copy. Counting is now a section of its own in the panel’s menu.
